Removed cleanly by `codegraph uninstall`. - Set up auto-allow permissions when Claude Code or Qwen Code is one of the targets The installer **wires up your agents only — it does not index your code.** After it finishes, build each project's graph yourself with `codegraph init` (step 3). One global `codegraph install` covers every project; you run `codegraph init` once per project. **Non-interactive (scripting / CI):** ```bash codegraph install --yes # auto-detect agents, install global codegraph install --yes --init # same, then build the current project's index (one-shot bootstrap) codegraph install --target=cursor,claude --yes # explicit target list codegraph install --target=auto --location=local # detected agents, project-local codegraph install --target=copilot-vscode,copilot-cli,copilot-jetbrains --yes # GitHub Copilot everywhere codegraph install --print-config codex # print snippet, no file writes codegraph install --print-config copilot-vscode # same, for Copilot in VS Code ``` | Flag | Values | Default | |---|---|---| | `--target` | `auto`, `all`, `none`, or csv (`claude,cursor,...`) | prompt | | `--location` | `global`, `local` | prompt | | `--yes` | (boolean) | prompt every step | | `--init` | (boolean) run `codegraph init` in the current directory after wiring agents | — | | `--no-permissions` | (boolean) skip the auto-allow list (Claude Code, Qwen Code) | permissions on | | `--print-config ` | dump snippet for one agent and exit | — | ### 2. Restart Your Agent Restart your agent (Claude Code / Cursor / Codex CLI / opencode / Hermes Agent / Gemini CLI / Antigravity IDE / Kiro / VS Code, the Copilot CLI, or your JetBrains IDE for GitHub Copilot / IBM Bob / Factory Droid / Windsurf / Qwen Code / DeepSeek Harness / Grok Build / Kimi Code / Qoder CLI / Pi) for the MCP server to load. ### 3. Initialize Projects ```bash cd your-project codegraph init ``` Builds the per-project knowledge graph index, which then auto-syncs on every file change. A single global `codegraph install` works in every project you open — no need to re-run the installer per project. Add `--yes` to skip every prompt (scripts / CI / container bootstraps). That's it — your agent will use CodeGraph tools automatically when a `.codegraph/` directory exists.
Manual Setup (Alternative) **Install globally:** ```bash npm install -g @colbymchenry/codegraph ``` **Add to `~/.claude.json`:** ```json { "mcpServers": { "codegraph": { "type": "stdio", "command": "codegraph", "args": ["serve", "--mcp"], "alwaysLoad": true } } } ``` `alwaysLoad` keeps `codegraph_explore` loaded from the first prompt. Claude Code otherwise defers every MCP tool behind a tool-search step, so a fresh session sees only the tool's name until the model searches for it. **Add to `~/.claude/settings.json` (optional, for auto-allow):** ```json { "permissions": { "allow": [ "mcp__codegraph__*" ] } } ``` One wildcard auto-approves every CodeGraph tool — `codegraph_explore` is the only one listed by default, but if you re-enable others via `CODEGRAPH_MCP_TOOLS` they're already permitted, no prompt.
Agent Tool Guidance CodeGraph's MCP server delivers its usage guidance to your agent **automatically**, in the MCP `initialize` response. In short, it tells the agent to: - **Answer structural questions directly with CodeGraph** — it *is* the pre-built index, so a grep/read loop just repeats work it already did. Treat the returned source as already read. - **Reach for `codegraph_explore` for almost anything** — "how does X work", a flow/"how does X reach Y", or surveying an area. One call returns the relevant symbols' verbatim source grouped by file, the call paths between them (dynamic-dispatch hops included), and a blast-radius summary. Name a file or symbol in the query to read its current line-numbered source. - **Trust the results — don't re-verify with grep**, and check the staleness banner after edits. - Works **per project**: query any project that has a `.codegraph/` index by passing `projectPath` — so a monorepo where only some services are indexed, or a second repo, works in one session. A path with no index returns clean guidance to use built-in tools; indexing stays your decision. The exact text is `src/mcp/server-instructions.ts` — the single source of truth for the main agent. Because subagents and non-MCP harnesses never see the MCP guidance, the installer also writes a short marker-fenced section into the agent's instructions file pointing at the `codegraph explore` CLI equivalent.
--- ## How It Works ``` ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Claude Code │ │ │ │ "How does a request reach the database?" │ │ calls CodeGraph tools directly — no Explore sub-agent │ │ │ │ └─────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ CodeGraph MCP Server │ │ │ │ explore · one call → verbatim source + call flow + blast radius │ │ │ │ │ ▼ │ │ SQLite knowledge graph │ │ symbols · edges · files · FTS5 full-text search │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` 1. **Extraction** — a native **Rust kernel** parses source with [tree-sitter](https://tree-sitter.github.io/) grammars compiled into it, extracting nodes (functions, classes, methods) and edges (calls, imports, extends, implements) for 20 languages; remaining languages and per-file fallbacks use the same extraction logic on the portable engine, producing identical graphs. 2. **Storage** — Everything goes into a local SQLite database (`.codegraph/codegraph.db`) with FTS5 full-text search. 3. **Resolution** — After extraction, references are resolved: function calls → definitions, imports → source files, class inheritance, and framework-specific patterns. 4. **Auto-Sync** — The MCP server watches your project using native OS file events. Changes are debounced (2-second quiet window), filtered to source files only, and incrementally synced. The graph stays fresh as you code — no configuration needed. --- ## CLI Reference ```bash codegraph # Run interactive installer codegraph install # Run installer (explicit) codegraph uninstall # Remove CodeGraph from your agents AND the CLI (--keep-cli for configs only) codegraph init [path] # Initialize a project + build its graph (one step; --local-only keeps .codegraph/ out of git) codegraph uninit [path] # Remove CodeGraph from a project (--force to skip prompt) codegraph index [path] # Rebuild the full index from scratch (--quiet for less output; --force to allow a home folder or drive root) codegraph sync [path] # Incremental update codegraph status [path] # Show statistics (--json, --strict) codegraph unlock [path] # Remove a stale lock file that's blocking indexing codegraph query # Search symbols (--kind, --limit, --json) codegraph explore # Relevant symbols' source + call paths in one shot (same output as the codegraph_explore MCP tool) codegraph context # Relevant symbols, relationships and code for a task description (--format markdown|json) codegraph node # One symbol's source + callers, or read a file with line numbers (same output as codegraph_node) codegraph files # Show file structure (--format tree|flat|grouped|package, --tests/--no-tests, --filter, --max-depth, --json) codegraph callers # Find what calls a function/method (--limit, --json) codegraph callees # Find what a function/method calls (--limit, --json) codegraph impact # Analyze what code is affected by changing a symbol (--depth, --json) codegraph implementations # List the types that implement or extend a type (--depth, --json) codegraph affected [files...] # Find test files affected by changes (see below) codegraph cycles [path] # List circular imports between files (--json); exits 1 when there are any codegraph daemon # Manage background daemons — pick one to stop (alias: daemons) codegraph telemetry [on|off] # Show or change anonymous usage telemetry codegraph upgrade [version] # Update to the latest release (--check, --force) codegraph version # Print the installed version (also -v, --version) codegraph help [command] # Show help, optionally for one command ``` ### `codegraph affected` Traces import dependencies transitively to find which test files are affected by changed source files. ```bash codegraph affected src/utils.ts src/api.ts # Pass files as arguments git diff --name-only | codegraph affected --stdin # Pipe from git diff codegraph affected src/auth.ts --filter "e2e/*" # Custom test file pattern ``` | Option | Description | Default | |--------|-------------|---------| | `--stdin` | Read file list from stdin | `false` | | `-d, --depth ` | Max dependency traversal depth | `5` | | `-f, --filter ` | Glob for the files that count as tests (see below) | auto-detect | | `-j, --json` | Output as JSON | `false` | | `-q, --quiet` | Output file paths only | `false` | | `--cross-tier` | Also follow links across a process boundary: a client's HTTP call to its server's route, a queue job to its consumer, an event to its handler | `false` | `--filter` matches the whole name. With no slash (`*_test.go`) it matches the file name at any depth, with a slash (`e2e/*.spec.ts`) that folder at any depth, and with a leading `/` (`/tests/**/*.py`) from the project root only. `**` also matches no folder, so `tests/**/*.py` includes `tests/test_x.py`. Without `--filter`, files with the usual test names and folders count as tests, Google-style `foo_unittest.cc` and `foo_unittest.py` included. **CI/hook example:** ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash AFFECTED=$(git diff --name-only HEAD | codegraph affected --stdin --quiet) if [ -n "$AFFECTED" ]; then npx vitest run $AFFECTED fi ``` --- ## MCP Tools When running as an MCP server, CodeGraph exposes a **single tool** — `codegraph_explore`. Measured agent behavior showed that one strong tool steers agents better than a menu of narrower ones — fewer mis-picks, and it saves context every session: | Tool | Purpose | |------|---------| | `codegraph_explore` | Answer almost any question in one call — "how does X work", a flow ("how does X reach Y"), or surveying an area — returning the relevant symbols' verbatim source grouped by file, plus the call paths between them and a blast-radius summary. Surfaces dynamic-dispatch hops (callbacks, React re-render, interface→impl) grep can't follow. Name a file or symbol in the query to read its current line-numbered source, the same shape the Read tool gives you. A query that names one symbol, like "who calls `toValidURL`?", gets that symbol's source and every line that uses it, each with the function it sits in and the line's text. | The other tools (`codegraph_node`, `codegraph_search`, `codegraph_callers`, `codegraph_callees`, `codegraph_impact`, `codegraph_files`, `codegraph_status`) stay fully functional but **unlisted by default** — everything they return already arrives inline on `codegraph_explore` (its blast-radius section, the relationship map, a symbol's body as its callee list). Re-enable any of them for the MCP surface with the `CODEGRAPH_MCP_TOOLS` environment variable (e.g. `CODEGRAPH_MCP_TOOLS=explore,node,search,callers`), or use their CLI equivalents (`codegraph node` / `query` / `callers` / `callees` / `impact` / `files` / `status`). Even when the server's own root has no `.codegraph/` index, the tools stay available: pass `projectPath` to query any indexed project — a sub-service in a monorepo, or a second repo — in the same session. A path that has no index returns clean guidance to use built-in tools instead, so nothing fails loudly, and indexing stays your decision. --- ## Library Usage CodeGraph can be embedded directly. The npm package re-exports its programmatic API, so both `import` and `require` resolve the `CodeGraph` class in your own process — handy for embedding it in an app (e.g. an Electron main process). ```typescript import CodeGraph from '@colbymchenry/codegraph'; // CommonJS works too: // const { CodeGraph } = require('@colbymchenry/codegraph'); const cg = await CodeGraph.init('/path/to/project'); // Or: const cg = await CodeGraph.open('/path/to/project'); await cg.indexAll({ onProgress: (p) => console.log(`${p.phase}: ${p.current}/${p.total}`) }); const results = cg.searchNodes('UserService'); const callers = cg.getCallers(results[0].node.id); const context = await cg.buildContext('fix login bug', { maxNodes: 20, includeCode: true, format: 'markdown' }); const impact = cg.getImpactRadius(results[0].node.id, 2); cg.watch(); // auto-sync on file changes cg.unwatch(); // stop watching cg.close(); ``` Lower-level building blocks are exported from the same entry point for callers that drive the graph directly: `DatabaseConnection`, `QueryBuilder`, `getDatabasePath`, `initGrammars` / `loadGrammarsForLanguages`, and `FileLock`. **Embedding requirements** - Install from npm (`npm i @colbymchenry/codegraph`) so the matching per-platform package — which carries the compiled library and its dependencies — is fetched alongside the shim. - The API runs on **your** runtime, so it needs **Node 22.5+** for the built-in `node:sqlite` (Electron qualifies when its bundled Node is 22.5+). The CLI and MCP server are unaffected — they run on the self-contained bundled runtime. - TypeScript types ship with the package. As with any Node-targeting library, keep `@types/node` available and `skipLibCheck: true` (the common default). --- ## Configuration Next to none — CodeGraph is **zero-config by default**, with nothing to write or keep in sync to get started. Language support is automatic from the file extension; there's nothing to wire up per language. The one optional file is for mapping [custom file extensions](#custom-file-extensions). What it skips out of the box: - **Dependency, build, and cache directories** — `node_modules`, `vendor`, `dist`, `build`, `target`, `.venv`, `Pods`, `.next`, and the like across every [supported stack](#supported-languages) — so the graph is your code, not third-party noise. This holds even with no `.gitignore`. A `build` folder inside `src/` is the exception: no build step writes TypeScript, JSX, Vue, Svelte, Astro, Go, C# or Rust files into one, so those are indexed from it, and a Java, Kotlin or Scala package named `build` is indexed whole. - **Anything in your `.gitignore`** — honored in git repos via git, and in non-git projects by reading `.gitignore` directly (root and nested). - **Files larger than 1 MB** — generated bundles, minified JS, vendored blobs. To keep something else out, add it to `.gitignore`. To pull a default-excluded directory back **in** (say you really do want a vendored dependency indexed), add a negation — `!vendor/`. The defaults apply uniformly, so committing a dependency or build directory doesn't force it into the graph; the `.gitignore` negation is the explicit opt-in. `.gitignore` can't drop a directory you've **committed**, though. For a vendored theme or SDK that's checked into the repo (e.g. a Metronic theme under `static/`), list it under `exclude` in `codegraph.json` — gitignore-style patterns, matched against repo-root-relative paths, honored on index, sync, and watch: ```json { "exclude": ["static/", "**/vendor/**"] } ``` Conversely, when real source is gitignored on purpose — a project under a second VCS (SVN, Perforce) that `.gitignore`s its own source so it stays out of Git — force it back in with `include` (the opposite of `exclude`; `includeIgnored` only revives embedded git repos, not plain source): ```json { "include": ["Tools/", "Local/typescript/"] } ``` CodeGraph discovers those files off disk, overriding `.gitignore`, on index, sync, and watch. An explicit `exclude` still wins, and built-in skips (`node_modules`, `dist`, `.git`) are never re-included. Sometimes a directory shouldn't leave the index — you still want to find things in it — it just shouldn't *outrank* your real code. A `scripts/` or `optional-skills/` tree whose helpers use generic names (`usage`, `status`, `run`) can win on an exact name match and crowd out the product code that actually answers the query. Name those trees under `deprioritize`: ```json { "deprioritize": ["optional-skills/", "scripts/"] } ``` This is the ranking counterpart to `exclude`: those paths stay indexed and findable — searching for them directly still works — they just stop winning against first-party code. It applies to `query` / `search` and to `explore`'s ranking. It is *not* a filter: unlike the built-in `example/`, `sample/`, `fixture/`, `benchmark/` and `demo/` handling — which also drops those files from some result sets outright — `deprioritize` only ever changes rank. Reach for `exclude` when you want something gone. ### Custom file extensions If your project uses a non-standard extension for a [supported language](#supported-languages) — say `.dota_lua` for Lua, or `.tpl` for PHP — those files are skipped by default, because the extension isn't one CodeGraph recognizes. Map them with an optional **`codegraph.json`** at your project root: ```json { "extensions": { ".dota_lua": "lua", ".tpl": "php" } } ``` Each value is a supported language id. The mappings merge on top of the built-in defaults and win on conflict, so you can also re-point a built-in (e.g. `".h": "cpp"`). Commit the file to share the mapping with your team. A typo'd language or a malformed file is warned about and skipped — it never breaks indexing — and a project with no `codegraph.json` behaves exactly as before. Re-index (`codegraph index`) after adding or changing mappings. ### PHP includes from the web root PHP code often loads files from the folder the web server serves, as in `require $_SERVER['DOCUMENT_ROOT'] . '/inc/header.php'`. That folder is set in the server's configuration, not in your code, so CodeGraph works it out from your includes: it's the folder under which their paths name files your project has. When they don't settle it (fewer than three different paths, or two folders that fit them about as well), name it in `codegraph.json`: ```json { "webRoot": "public" } ``` The folder is relative to the project root, like `"public"`, `"web"` or `"htdocs"`, or `"."` for the root itself, and a `webRoot` you set always wins. Without either, these includes link to nothing rather than to a guess, which could be a different file of the same name. The next sync applies a change. Includes built from the including file's own folder, like `__DIR__ . '/inc/a.php'`, need neither. ## Telemetry CodeGraph collects **anonymous usage statistics** — which tools and commands get used, which languages get indexed — to guide where language and agent support work goes. **Never** any code, paths, file or symbol names, queries, or IP addresses; usage is aggregated locally into daily totals before anything is sent, and the ingest endpoint is [public code in this repo](telemetry-worker/) that enforces the documented field list. The installer asks up front; turn it off any time: ```bash codegraph telemetry off # or: CODEGRAPH_TELEMETRY=0, or DO_NOT_TRACK=1 ``` To turn it off for one MCP server entry only, such as one in a config you share, add `--no-telemetry` to its arguments: `codegraph serve --mcp --no-telemetry`. That covers the background server it starts too. [`TELEMETRY.md`](TELEMETRY.md) lists every field, with the off-switches and the full data-handling story. ## Verified releases Every artifact is built and published by the public [Release workflow](.github/workflows/release.yml) — never from a laptop — and carries cryptographic proof of it: - **npm packages** are published via [trusted publishing](https://docs.npmjs.com/trusted-publishers) (OIDC — no long-lived npm tokens exist that could be stolen) with [provenance attestations](https://docs.npmjs.com/generating-provenance-statements) linking every version to the exact commit and workflow run that built it. Verify what's installed: ```bash npm audit signatures ``` - **GitHub Release bundles** (and `SHA256SUMS`) carry signed [build attestations](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-for-github-actions/using-artifact-attestations) (SLSA v1.0 Build Level 2). Verify any downloaded bundle: ```bash gh attestation verify codegraph-darwin-arm64.tar.gz -R colbymchenry/codegraph ``` - **The bundled Node.js runtime** is checked against the SHA-256 checksums nodejs.org publishes before it goes into a bundle. Releases published before July 2026 predate this pipeline and don't carry attestations. ## Supported Platforms Every release ships a self-contained build (bundled Node runtime — nothing to compile) for all three desktop OSes, on both Intel/AMD (x64) and ARM (arm64): | Platform | Architectures | Install | |----------|---------------|---------| | Windows | x64, arm64 | PowerShell installer or npm | | macOS | x64, arm64 | shell installer or npm | | Linux | x64, arm64 | shell installer or npm | See [Get Started](#get-started) for the one-line install commands. ## Supported Agents The interactive installer auto-detects and configures each of these — wiring up the MCP server, which delivers its own usage guidance. For Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, opencode, Factory Droid, Qwen Code, DeepSeek Harness, Grok Build, Kimi Code and Pi it also writes a short marker-fenced CodeGraph section into the agent's instructions file (`CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` / `GEMINI.md` / `QWEN.md`, or `rules/codegraph.md` for Grok Build), so subagents and non-MCP agents learn the `codegraph explore` command: - **Claude Code** - **Cursor** - **Codex CLI** — the Codex IDE extension reads the same config: a global install writes `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml` (default `~/.codex/config.toml`), and a local install writes `.codex/config.toml`, which Codex uses only in a project you've marked as trusted - **opencode** — MCP entry is OpenCode 2's `mcp.servers.codegraph` with `codemode: false` (keeps `codegraph_explore` on the native tool list; `codegraph install` migrates the older `mcp.codegraph` shape) - **Hermes Agent** - **Gemini CLI** - **Antigravity IDE** - **Kiro** - **GitHub Copilot** — Copilot Chat in VS Code (`copilot-vscode`), the Copilot CLI (`copilot-cli`), and the Copilot plugin in JetBrains IDEs (`copilot-jetbrains`) - **IBM Bob** (`bob`) — Bob IDE and Bob Shell: `~/.bob/settings/mcp.json`, or `.bob/mcp.json` in a project - **Factory Droid** (`droid`) — `~/.factory/mcp.json`, or `.factory/mcp.json`, which is meant to be committed; Droid reloads the file on its own - **Windsurf** (`windsurf`) — global only: `~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json`, which Devin, Windsurf's new name, imports by default - **Qwen Code** (`qwen`) — `settings.json` in `$QWEN_HOME` (default `~/.qwen`) or `.qwen/`, keeping any comments in it - **DeepSeek Harness** (`dsh`) — global only: one entry in `$DSH_HOME/cordis.patch.yml` (default `~/.dsh`) covers every profile - **Grok Build** (`grok`) — `$GROK_HOME/config.toml` (default `~/.grok`), or `.grok/config.toml`, which Grok uses only in a trusted folder - **Kimi Code** (`kimi`) — `$KIMI_CODE_HOME/mcp.json` (default `~/.kimi-code`), or `.kimi-code/mcp.json`, which Kimi Code uses only in a trusted folder - **Qoder CLI** (`qoder`) — `$QODER_CONFIG_DIR/settings.json` (default `~/.qoder`), or `.qoder/settings.local.json`; in the Qoder IDE, add the server under Settings > MCP - **Pi** (`pi`) — `mcp.json` in Pi's agent directory (default `~/.pi/agent`), or `.pi/mcp.json`, which Pi reads once you trust the project; `exposure: "direct"` keeps `codegraph_explore` on the model's tool list ## Supported Languages | Language | Extension | Status | |----------|-----------|--------| | TypeScript | `.ts`, `.tsx` | Full support | | JavaScript | `.js`, `.jsx`, `.mjs` | Full support | | ArkTS (HarmonyOS) | `.ets` | Full support (everything TypeScript has, plus `@Component`/`@ComponentV2` structs with their ArkUI decorators (`@State`/`@Prop`/`@Link`/`@Local`/`@Builder`/…), `build()` view trees — parent→child component edges, chained-attribute links to `@Extend`/`@Styles` functions, `.onClick(this.handler)` event bindings — dynamic-dispatch bridges for state→`build()` re-renders, `@ohos.events.emitter` emit→subscriber pairs (static event keys only), and `router.pushUrl` literal urls → the target page struct; ohpm workspace modules resolve bare `import { X } from "data"` through `oh-package.json5` `file:` dependencies, honoring each module's `main` entry) | | Python | `.py` | Full support | | Go | `.go` | Full support | | Rust | `.rs` | Full support | | Java | `.java` | Full support | | C# | `.cs` | Full support (MediatR `Send` / `Publish` link to their handlers, including ones written against your own interfaces like `ICommandHandler` or a package's) | | ASP.NET Razor / Blazor | `.cshtml`, `.razor` | Markup links: `@model`, `@inherits`, `@inject`, `@typeof` and Blazor component tags link to the C# types they name, and what an inline `

repositories.name: LoopForge
repositories.description: Self-hosted workflows for coding-agent delivery. Orchestrate CodeBuddy, Codex and Claude Code with scripts and human approval gates. Includes Local workflows for coding assistants.
repositories.readme:
English · 简体中文

Two ways to work · Quick start · LOOPs · Features · Local (Legacy) · FAQ · Docs

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8af401d9-1aae-427c-b4bc-455c12d17beb

80-second product tour (1080p, with sound).

**LoopForge** is a self-hosted workspace where your team ships software with coding agents. Describe what you need to **Main Bot** in chat: it opens a Docker sandbox, checks out your repositories, delegates to project roles, and opens the PR. When a way of working proves itself, save it as a **LOOP** (a reusable delivery workflow of agents, scripts and human gates) so the next requirement is delivered the same way, with review and approval built in. Coding-agent CLIs do the work: CodeBuddy, Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Cursor CLI, Antigravity, Kimi Code, Pi, DeepSeek Harness and ZCode. LoopForge adds the roles, sandboxes, checkpoints and history around them, all on your own infrastructure under the MIT license. ## Two ways to work | | **Chat with Main Bot** | **Run a LOOP** | | --- | --- | --- | | Best for | Exploring, quick fixes, iterating with the agent | Repeatable delivery with fixed stages and sign-off | | How it runs | Main Bot opens a [conversation workspace](docs/conversation-workspaces.md) (a Docker sandbox with your repos) on demand and calls project roles as subagents | The engine runs Agent, Script, Human-gate and sub-LOOP nodes in order, in their own sandbox | | You stay in control by | Queuing or steering messages mid-reply, and pausing, resuming or taking over a running LOOP from chat | Approving at human gates, sending work back to a chosen step, retrying or rerunning from any node | | Delivers | A PR/MR, or a direct merge into a shared branch (`mode=direct`) | Documents, code or a PR, plus per-node artifacts and logs | Both paths track the same **requirements**, so every change, whether made in chat or by a LOOP, links back to what was asked for and counts toward delivery and cost reports.

The chat home. Type a request, @ a role, skill, requirement, LOOP or repository, and pick the executor, model and permission mode per conversation.

## Why LoopForge Ask a coding agent to "fix this bug" and the result depends on that run. It might skip the plan, forget the tests, review its own code, or stop halfway without anyone noticing. That's fine for a demo, but it isn't how a team ships. - **Repeatable.** Same LOOP, same stages, same checks for every requirement. Start from built-in backend, frontend, bug-fix and product LOOPs. - **Separated roles.** Planning, implementation, review and testing each get their own prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills and MCP tools. A role works as a LOOP node or as a subagent in chat. - **Human on the loop.** Agents run on their own while you supervise. Pause, steer or take over anytime, and approval gates stop the run where a human must decide: approve, or send the work back to a chosen step. - **Observable and resumable.** Node status, tool traces, logs and artifacts in one place. Pause, retry a failed step, or rerun from any node. - **Your stack, your servers.** Ten coding-agent CLIs as executors, from CodeBuddy, Codex and Claude Code to OpenCode, Cursor CLI and more. GitHub, Skills and MCP as tools. Docker sandboxes or your own machine as the runtime. ## Quick start Install **Git** and clone the repository first. The installer checks Docker, Compose, Python 3 and curl and offers to install missing components. Python/curl installation supports apt, dnf and yum on Linux; the Compose plugin supports x86_64/arm64 and verifies the official release SHA-256. macOS needs a working Python 3 and Docker Desktop; Homebrew can install missing components. Ordinary Linux users are supported through Docker group access or sudo. Set `LOOPFORGE_YES=1` to accept installation prompts. Package and image downloads require internet access. ```bash git clone https://github.com/Tencent/LoopForge.git cd LoopForge ./start.sh ``` `./start.sh` pulls the GHCR release image pinned in `compose.yaml` without building locally (`bash scripts/install.sh` does the same). It creates the MySQL and platform services, generates configuration and session secrets, and installs the built-in sandboxes, starter LOOPs and welcome project. Host Go and Node.js installations are not required. Configure model API keys and GitHub authorization after startup. Use `./start.sh logs`, `stop`, `restart` or `pull` to manage it, and `./start.sh dev` to build the checkout from source. If downloads from `ghcr.io` stall, `./start.sh` and `./start.sh pull` time `ghcr.io` against the Nanjing University mirror [ghcr.nju.edu.cn](https://doc.nju.edu.cn/books/e1654/page/ghcr). Nanjing is used only when its manifest digest matches the digest just read from ghcr.io; the script pulls that digest and tags it back to the name pinned in `compose.yaml`, which trusts that host because the result is tagged with the official name. A missing official digest, a mismatch, or a failed mirror pull stays on `ghcr.io`. `MIRROR=ghcr.io` forces the upstream registry and `MIRROR=ghcr.nju.edu.cn` forces Nanjing; the choice is not written to `.env`. The GitHub Release records the digest; `docker image inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' ghcr.io/tencent/loopforge:` should show the same digest after `@`. `compose.yaml` stays unchanged. A Docker `registry-mirrors` entry such as `https://docker.nju.edu.cn` only accelerates Docker Hub and is not a value for `MIRROR`. ```bash ./start.sh MIRROR=ghcr.io ./start.sh MIRROR=ghcr.nju.edu.cn ./start.sh pull ``` Open the address printed by the installer and create your account; the first one becomes the administrator. The service listens on `0.0.0.0:8090` by default. On a cloud host, the installer reads the public IP from the provider's metadata service and prints it; allow the port in your security group, or put an HTTPS reverse proxy in front. Restrict access to your own IP until the administrator account exists. The home page's quick-access guide walks you through adding a model key, connecting a repository and choosing a LOOP. For GitLab, Gitea, Gogs and other Git hosts, [set up Git SSH](docs/deployment.md#git-repositories-over-ssh) to check out and push branches with a personal key. PR/MR and Issue automation requires a hosting API token or a separately configured MCP. ### Try it without an API key New accounts join the **LoopForge demo project**, which includes a LOOP made only of a script and a human gate: 1. Switch to the demo project, open **Templates**, and open **Platform check · script & approval**. 2. Click **Run LOOP**. A real script writes a report, then the run waits for you at the approval step. 3. Approve it from **Needs review** or the run page, and watch the run continue to its final artifact. ### What you need for real work | I want to… | You need | | --- | --- | | Run the script + approval demo | Nothing | | Chat with Main Bot, generate a document or a new project | An API key for the selected executor | | Change an existing repository (in chat or via a LOOP) and open a PR | Model credentials and a GitHub repository (connect GitHub in personal settings) |
More setup details: executors, GitHub, sandboxes, access model
- **Executors.** Choose a CLI and model for chat, requirement clarification, Bot replies, notification reports, run evaluation, or static preview. Each LOOP role can select its own CLI, and built-in templates still default to CodeBuddy. Scheduled prompts use the CLI selected on the schedule. The platform can run without a CodeBuddy installation or key once its workflows use other CLIs. [Deployment and upgrade](docs/deployment.md#choosing-an-executor) | Executor | Credentials | Installation | | --- | --- | --- | | **CodeBuddy** | Personal key, or a shared key an administrator configures for chat and LOOP runs | Bundled by default, optional on source builds | | **Codex** | Personal key; a connected execution machine can use its local login | In the Docker image | | **Claude Code** | Personal key; a connected execution machine can use its local login | Installed from npm on first use, then cached | | **OpenCode · Kimi Code · Pi** | Personal key only | Installed from npm on first use, then cached | | **DeepSeek Harness** | Personal key only | In the Docker image | | **Cursor CLI** | Personal key only | Provider installer on first chat use; not installed into LOOP sandboxes | | **Antigravity** | Personal key, or the connected execution machine owner's existing account login | Install the official CLI on the execution machine and in Docker images used for LOOP runs | | **ZCode** | Personal key only | Not bundled; install it on the service or execution machine PATH | The seven agent CLIs after Claude Code keep their model and MCP configuration in a private home directory per run. Antigravity can reuse the execution machine owner's account login in conversation workspaces and native or Docker LOOP sandboxes. Its official CLI refreshes the credential copy, and the Runner saves the refreshed login back to its original local store. Gemini API keys use separate API billing. The other agent CLIs use the responsible user's own key and Base URL from personal settings, including on a connected execution machine. First-use installs need npm or provider access; [native deployments](docs/deployment.md#workers-and-runners) need the CLI for the executor you choose. - **WeCom notifications.** The image built from this Dockerfile includes `wecom-cli`; published images gain it with the next release. Native installations need to install it separately; see [Deployment](docs/deployment.md#native-development). - **GitHub is optional.** All built-in generic LOOPs run without a repository: product LOOPs deliver documents, and new frontend/backend projects deliver source files in the task workspace. Bug fixes still need source code and reproduction details. Connect a repository when you work on existing code or want PRs. - **Delivering to a repository.** Choose **Connect GitHub** in personal settings, approve the device code on GitHub and pick your repository (the LoopForge OAuth App is built in; no PAT required, manual PAT entry still works). Set executor credentials (or bind a local execution machine), then either run a project LOOP or ask Main Bot to change the code and submit a PR/MR. - **Sandboxes.** In the default Compose installation, LOOP runs and conversation workspaces both use Docker sandbox containers started through the host Docker socket. Default sandboxes reuse the installed runtime image, so nothing extra is built after installation; custom Dockerfiles still build their own images. Docker socket access grants control of the host daemon, so this setup is for trusted teams, not untrusted multi-tenant isolation. See [deployment boundaries](docs/deployment.md#accounts). Re-running the installer keeps your data. - **Accounts and access.** New installations listen on all interfaces (existing bind settings are kept) and are designed for a trusted team: signed-in users can read project data across the instance, and teammates can sign up from the login page (`AGENTFLOW_ALLOW_SIGNUP=false` in `.env` turns that off). Read the [account and access model](docs/deployment.md#accounts) before exposing it beyond your team. - **Remote access, HTTPS, separate workers.** See [Deployment](docs/deployment.md). - **Hacking on LoopForge itself?** `bash scripts/dev.sh` runs it natively (Go 1.26.11+).
## How LOOPs work A **LOOP** is the workflow a delivery follows. Agents, scripts and people take part in the same run:

The LOOP designer with a project copy of the built-in bug-fix LOOP. Each step picks a role; failed checks can send the work back to an earlier step.

| Node | What it does | | --- | --- | | **Agent** | A role (prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills and MCP tools) that designs, implements, reviews or tests. | | **Script** | A deterministic shell step: build, test, lint, generate a report. No AI where AI is not needed. | | **Human gate** | Pauses the run until someone checks the artifacts and approves, or sends the work back to a step. | | **Sub-LOOP** | Runs another LOOP as a sub-workflow. | | **Preview build** | Builds a static site and archives it for review. | Each node declares its artifacts and dependencies, and the engine starts each step once its dependencies complete. Start from a built-in LOOP, adapt its roles, rules and environment to your project, and publish versions as it evolves.

A run waiting at a human gate: approve and continue, add context and rerun the step, or send the work back upstream.

**A delivery we actually ran:** four CodeBuddy roles planned a Python fix, implemented it, reviewed it independently and summarized the delivery. Three real tests passed; the run waited for human approval, then verified the accepted code had not changed. The [reusable acceptance case](e2e/api/45-delivery-model.test.mjs) checks the files and results. See the [validation record](docs/validation.md) for scope and known gaps. ## Features | Area | What you get | | --- | --- | | **Chat workbench** | Main Bot with per-conversation executor, model and permission mode. `@` references for roles, skills, requirements, LOOPs and repositories. Messages queue while a reply runs; *Steer* interrupts and sends now. Generated files open in a side panel with preview, source and download. | | **Conversation workspaces** | On-demand Docker sandboxes with the project's repositories checked out, project roles as native subagents, and direct control of a running LOOP workspace: pause, resume or take over. | | **LOOP designer** | Visual canvas with Agent, Script, Human gate, Sub-LOOP and Preview nodes, rework-on-failure edges, validation, version history and publishing. Built-in backend, frontend, bug-fix and product LOOPs. | | **Roles** | Reusable definitions: prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills, MCP tools, artifacts and gates, shared across LOOP nodes and chat subagents. | | **Requirement → delivery** | Requirements tracked end to end, whether shipped by a LOOP or straight from chat, with PR/MR status tracking, merge detection and direct-branch merges. | | **Runs & approvals** | Live node status, tool traces, worker logs, per-node artifact snapshots and workspace previews. A single **Needs review** inbox for every gate waiting on you. | | **AI scheduled tasks** | Recurring agent tasks with full workspace, LOOP and MCP access; a shared market of versioned, parameterized task templates; automatic LOOP dispatch for new requirements. | | **Insights & cost** | Engineering metrics, business-domain reports with static HTML/SVG export, and token/cost accounting for LOOPs and conversations at public list prices. | | **Execution environments** | Platform workers, Docker sandboxes, or a connected local execution machine using your own tools and repositories. | | **Team-ready** | Password accounts, projects and members, light/dark/system themes, an OpenAPI-described HTTP and MCP API. Management pages are in English and Chinese; the chat workbench is Chinese for now. |

Built-in LOOPs are read-only blueprints; copy one into your project to run and edit it.

## LoopForge Local > **Legacy.** Previously published versions of LoopForge Local (`loopforge-cli`) remain available. The [Local guide](docs/local/usage.md) covers installing a fixed version and keeping existing workflows and artifacts. To use platform projects and LOOPs from a coding assistant, [connect CodeBuddy to your LoopForge instance over MCP](docs/local/usage.md#connect-to-loopforge-with-mcp). Local continues to run its built-in workflows inside the coding assistant without a LoopForge server. | | Platform | Local (Legacy) | | --- | --- | --- | | Best for | Teams sharing chat workspaces, LOOPs, approvals and history | One developer inside an IDE or CLI | | Needs | Docker + Python 3 | Node.js 20+, Python 3.8+ and a coding assistant | | Workflows | Chat with Main Bot + custom LOOPs on a visual canvas | Built-in Classic / Portable workflows | | Evidence | Shared run details, approvals and metrics in the web workspace | Artifacts under `artifacts/{task_slug}/` + optional local dashboard | ## FAQ **Do I need an API key to try it?** No. The demo LOOP uses only a script and a human gate. Chat and agent steps need a key for the executor you pick. Model usage is not included; you bring your own credentials. **Do I need GitHub?** No. Chat, documents and new projects run in the task workspace. Connect GitHub when you want to change an existing repository or open PRs. **Should I use chat or a LOOP?** Use chat to explore and iterate; Main Bot can still open a PR. Once you find a way of working you want every requirement to follow, with fixed reviewers, tests and sign-off, put it in a LOOP. Main Bot can start, pause and take over LOOP runs, so the two paths work together. **How is this different from Dify, n8n or Flowise?** Those are general-purpose AI and automation workflow builders. LoopForge is built for **software delivery with coding agents**: implementer and reviewer roles, Docker sandboxes with real repositories, GitHub delivery, human acceptance gates and run evidence. **How is this different from using Claude Code, Codex, CodeBuddy or another coding CLI directly?** LoopForge doesn't replace them; it orchestrates them. Each agent step and each chat turn runs one of those CLIs. LoopForge adds what surrounds it: who does what, in which sandbox, in which order, with which checks, and who signs off. **Is it safe to expose on the internet?** New installations listen on all interfaces and target a trusted team. Read the [account and access model](docs/deployment.md#accounts) and set up HTTPS before opening it up. Report vulnerabilities privately via the [security policy](SECURITY.md). ## Documentation | I want to… | Start here | | --- | --- | | Deploy, manage accounts, connect execution machines | [Deployment](docs/deployment.md) | | Understand chat workspaces, scheduled AI tasks and token pricing | [Conversation workspaces](docs/conversation-workspaces.md) · [AI scheduled tasks](docs/ai-scheduled-task-capabilities.md) · [Token pricing](docs/token-pricing.md) | | Maintain an existing Local installation | [LoopForge Local](docs/local/usage.md) · [Editions](docs/local/editions.md) | | Extend the platform or use the HTTP / MCP API | [Architecture](docs/architecture.md) · [API reference](docs/api/README.md) · [Shared schedules API](docs/api/shared-schedules.md) | | Contribute to the UI | [Frontend design conventions](design.md) (Chinese) | | Check functional coverage and release readiness | [Validation record](docs/validation.md) · [Acceptance matrix](docs/testing/acceptance-matrix.md) · [Release review](docs/release-readiness.md) | | Understand source provenance and maintenance | [Public scope](docs/open-source-scope.md) · [Upstream synchronization](docs/upstream-sync.md) | ## Community Scan the QR code to join the LoopForge community group. ## Contributing Issues and PRs are welcome: share a use case, report a bug, or improve workflows, integrations and the platform experience. Start with the [contributing guide](CONTRIBUTING.md). Security issues go through the [security policy](SECURITY.md). If LoopForge is useful to you, a star helps others find it. ## License [MIT](LICENSE). Third-party components keep their own licenses and notices; see [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

repositories.name: Search
repositories.description: A small, fast WebKit browser for macOS, by Office Commun.
repositories.readme:
# Search

A small, fast, quiet web browser for the Mac, by [Office Commun](https://officecommun.com).

![Search, with its tabs down the left and a page taking the rest of the window](.github/screenshot.png)

**[Download for macOS →](https://searchbrowser.app)** · macOS 14 or later · free · about 14 MB

Or with [Homebrew](https://brew.sh): `brew install --cask driceroland/tap/search`

---

## What it is

Search is a browser with nothing in the way. A row of tabs — down the left, or across the top if you prefer — and the page. There is no toolbar, no start page, no sidebar of suggestions, no account to sign into, nothing that wants your attention. You type an address or a few words in one field and you are on the page.

It uses **WebKit**, the engine already inside every Mac (it is what Safari runs on). That is why the whole app is about 14 MB on disk and opens instantly: there is no second copy of Chromium to download, update and keep in memory.

It was built by a design studio that spends its whole day in a browser and was tired of the ones that had become products. This one is a tool.

## What it does

- **One field.** Type an address and you go there; type words and you search. It finishes addresses from your own history and never sends what you type anywhere until you press Return.
- **Tabs that stay out of the way.** Pin the pages you keep open all day and they shrink to a letter or their icon. Tabs from your last session come back instantly and cost nothing until you click them. `⌘K` lists your open tabs by name.
- **Keep an important site running.** Enable Keep selected sites awake in Settings › Tabs, then choose Keep This Site Awake in the site card. It prevents sleeping and automatic closure, even under memory pressure, at the cost of more memory. Private choices last only in that tab; manual closing still works.
- **Two pages side by side.** Turn on Split View in Settings › Tabs, then drag a tab onto a page or choose Tabs › Split Current Page. Drag the divider to resize the panes; the outlined pane receives page commands. Pairs and their widths come back with their Space, including after a restart.
- **Reading mode.** `⇧⌘R` strips a page down to the article.
- **Hide anything, for good.** `⇧⌘H`, then click a cookie banner, a newsletter overlay, a rail of "related" nonsense — it goes, and it is still gone on that site next time, before the page has drawn a single frame.
- **An ad blocker that runs before the page.** Third-party trackers and ad networks are stopped at the network level, so there is nothing to render and nothing to slow down. On by default, off per site if something breaks.
- **Video that follows you.** `⇧⌘P` lifts the video out of the page into a small window that stays above everything, including other apps.
- **Passwords, in your keychain.** Search offers to save a sign-in once it has actually worked, and offers your saved accounts, and the Mac's passkeys for the site, under the field when you click it — the way Safari does, never filling anything on its own. Everything lives in the macOS keychain, encrypted by the system, readable only by Search. Bring yours in from Chrome, Arc, Dia, Brave or Edge in one click; nothing leaves the Mac. Keep them in Apple's Passwords app instead? Turn it on in Settings › Passwords and its accounts and verification codes come up under their box too.
- **Light, dark, or the Mac's own.** The frame and the pages follow.
- **A wall behind the blank tab, if you like.** Settings › Themes paints it with a scenic mural, a pack of stickers, a colour, a gradient or a picture of your own, in light and dark, drawn once and kept so it costs nothing while you browse. Off until you choose one.
- **Bookmarks, history, downloads** — each a panel, each searchable, each one keystroke away.
- **Chrome extensions, without Chrome.** Paste a Chrome Web Store link in Settings › Extensions, or open the extension's page in Search and press Add. It runs on WebKit's own extension engine — the one Safari uses — and where Chrome has APIs WebKit doesn't (bookmarks, history, downloads, side panel, offscreen documents, fonts, notifications, speech, OAuth sign-in), Search fills them in itself. They live behind the puzzle button; pin the ones you use often. Building your own? Load its folder as an unpacked extension and press Reload after each change, as in Chrome's developer mode. macOS 15.4 or later.
- **Updates itself, quietly.** Once a day it checks for a newer build, downloads it, verifies it is signed by Office Commun, and swaps it in for the next launch. Nothing restarts on its own.

## What it doesn't do

On purpose:

- No extension you have to install to feel at home. Blocking ads, hiding clutter, reading mode, picture-in-picture and passwords are built in; extensions are there for everything else.
- No account and no cloud of ours. Your history and passwords are on your Mac and nowhere else. Sync with iCloud keeps your open tabs, pins, spaces, bookmarks and a few settings in your own iCloud, end to end encrypted: on for a new install once you leave the welcome, where its switch is, and off for a Search you had before until you turn it on.
- No telemetry, no analytics, no crash reports sent anywhere. The only things that leave your Mac are the pages you ask for, their icons, one small request a day to see whether there is a newer version, and, while they are on, Sync with iCloud and Handoff (below).
- One window. Tabs are the only kind of "new" there is.

## Privacy, concretely

| What | Where it is | Who can read it |
|---|---|---|
| Passwords | The macOS login keychain, as ordinary keychain items tagged `Search` | Search, signed by Office Commun. Any other app triggers the system's permission dialog. |
| History, bookmarks, open tabs, hidden elements | Small JSON files in `~/Library/Application Support/Search/` | You. |
| Cookies and site data | WebKit's own store for the app | The sites that set them, as in any browser. |
| Extensions | Unpacked in `~/Library/Application Support/Search/Extensions/`, their data in WebKit's extension store | Each extension, within the permissions you accepted when adding it. |
| News by email, the iPhone beta | Only if you type your email and press Join or Ask (the What's New card, the welcome, Settings › About): one HTTPS POST to searchbrowser.app with the address, where you pressed (`app-whats-new`, `app-welcome`, `app-settings`), which Mac download you have and, if ticked, that you want the iPhone beta. Your Mac keeps two yes/no flags, never the address. See `OptIn.swift`. | Office Commun, to send those emails through Resend; every one has a link to stop them, and hello@searchbrowser.app removes the address. |
| Sync with iCloud | While it is on (Settings › General; on for a new install from the moment you leave the welcome, off for a Search you had before until you turn it on): open tabs, pins, spaces, bookmarks, your search engine (and its suggestions address) and look, in Search's own zone of your private iCloud database, their contents end to end encrypted. Never private tabs, history, passwords, cookies or sign-ins. See `SYNC.md` and `ICloudSync.swift`. | You, on your devices signed in to your Apple Account. Not Office Commun: there is no server of ours. |
| Handoff | While it is on (Settings › General; on for a new install from the moment you leave the welcome, off for a Search you had before until you turn it on): the address and title of the page in front, handed to macOS, which offers it to your iPhone, iPad and other Macs. Never a private tab. See `Handoff.swift`. | Your devices signed in to your Apple Account, through Apple's Handoff. |
| Anything else | Nowhere. There is no server. | — |

A **private tab** (`⇧⌘N`) has its own cookie jar and leaves nothing behind when it closes.

Apps you allow in System Settings › Privacy & Security › Automation can read the address and title of your tabs with AppleScript, and the name of the space and profile each window is in; private tabs are never shown, and a window with one in front shows neither name.

## Keyboard

| | |
|---|---|
| `⌘L` address · `⌘K` switch tab · `⌘T` new tab · `⌘W` close · `⇧⌘T` reopen | `⌘[` `⌘]` back, forward · `⇧⌘[` `⇧⌘]` previous, next tab · `⌘1`–`⌘9` jump |
| `⇧⌘S` tabs down the left or across the top · `⌘S` fold the sidebar away · `⇧⌘B` bookmark this page | `⇧⌘R` reading mode · `⇧⌘P` float the video · `⇧⌘H` hide something · `⇧⌘U` what is hidden here |
| `⌘F` find · `⌘D` duplicate tab · `⇧⌘C` copy address · `⇧⌘V` paste and go | `⌘Y` history · `⇧⌘J` downloads · `⌘,` settings · `⌥⌘L` passwords |

Space keys (Control+1–9 by default) and the modifier used to peek at a link can be changed in Settings › Shortcuts while those features are enabled.

`⌘R` reloads the page; `⌥⌘R` reloads it from origin, checking everything cached with the site again, as Safari's Reload Page From Origin, which is also in a right-click on the reload button.

`⌃Tab` and `⌃⇧Tab` walk along the row of tabs; `Tab` stays the page's, for moving through a form. `esc` puts away whatever is open.

With Split View on, `⌥⌘N` splits the current page and `⌃⌘←` / `⌃⌘→` go from one page to the other. `⌘W` closes the focused tab and gives the remaining page the whole area. Tabs › Separate Split Tabs keeps both tabs open separately.

---

## For developers

### Why the source is here

So anyone can read exactly what a browser handling their passwords and history is doing, build it themselves, or fix something that bothers them. The code is small enough to actually read — about 42,000 lines of Swift, no dependencies beyond what Apple ships with macOS, one file per concern.

### Building it

- macOS 14 or later, Xcode 16 / Swift 6 toolchain
- `swift build` — runs the app straight from the SwiftPM binary
- `./build.sh` — assembles a real, double-clickable `Search.app` in `build/`, ad-hoc signed so it runs on your own Mac. `SEARCH_DEV=1 ./build.sh` makes it a dev build, on a yellow icon and named for its branch (`Search-split-view` from `claude/split-view-4a6927`), so it's never mistaken for an installed Search or for another worktree's build; `SEARCH_FEATURE=name` picks the name. It shares the installed app's settings and its bundle id, so while both run, a link from another app may land in either

A build you make yourself won't be notarized or carry Office Commun's Developer ID, so the first launch needs a right-click → Open (or an allow in System Settings → Privacy & Security). That's expected — it's the same thing that happens with any app that isn't from the App Store or a notarized DMG. Your own build also keeps its passwords apart from a signed Search's: the keychain tells the two apart by their signatures.

`./build.sh release dmg` also makes `Search.dmg` / `Search.zip`. `./build.sh release ship` additionally notarizes and staples — that step needs a Developer ID certificate and Apple credentials, so it only really does anything for Office Commun's own releases.

### How it's put together

- **SwiftUI** for everything drawn, **AppKit** for the handful of things SwiftUI doesn't reach on macOS (the window's title bar, dragging the window by an empty part of the tab row), **WKWebView** for pages.
- One `Tab` per page. Its web view is built lazily — a tab restored from last session doesn't cost a process until you switch to it. That's most of why launching with twenty tabs is still instant. Each page runs in WebKit's own content process, as in Safari; a tab you close is really gone.
- The ad blocker is a `WKContentRuleList` compiled once at launch and enforced inside WebKit's networking, before a request is made — zero cost at run time, unlike a JavaScript blocker.
- Hidden elements are a per-site list of selectors injected as a stylesheet at document start, so nothing is ever seen appearing and vanishing.
- Every colour is a light/dark pair in `Design.swift`, resolved by the window's appearance; nothing else in the code knows which mode it is in.
- Extensions run on `WKWebExtension` (macOS 15.4+). `Crx.swift` fetches an extension from the Chrome Web Store's public update address and checks the CRX3 signature against the extension's id before anything is unpacked. `Extensions.swift` is the browser's side of WebKit's contract — tabs, the window, permissions, popups. `ExtensionShims.swift` adds, at install, a small script to the extension's worker, pages and content scripts: it defines the Chrome APIs WebKit lacks — `userScripts`, `privacy`, `browsingData`, `sessions`, the old FileSystem API and more — as calls answered natively by Search, and mends the places where WebKit behaves differently from Chrome: replies from pages that don't answer, listeners added after a worker starts, workers WebKit loses track of, members and constants it leaves out. Extension pages are served from `chrome-extension://<id>/`, the address they have in Chrome, so servers and sites recognise them. `./bench ext-*` drives all of it from the shell against a test run. `ExtensionNative.swift` speaks Chrome's native messaging to hosts registered in Chrome's `NativeMessagingHosts` folders.
- `Sources/Search/` is one file per concern: `Vault.swift` is the keychain, `Shield.swift` the ad blocker, `Curtain.swift` the hidden elements, `Session.swift` what comes back at launch, `Updater.swift` the update, `Bench.swift` the test socket, and so on. There's no framework of its own to learn first.

### Testing it without closing it

Turn on **Settings › General › Let a script drive Search** and the running app listens on a Unix socket in its own folder (readable by your user only). `./bench` at the root of the repository speaks it:

```
./bench open https://example.com     # a tab of its own, at the end of your row, marked with a flask
./bench wait 2e7e7e89                 # until it has loaded
./bench text 2e7e7e89                 # the page's text
./bench shot 2e7e7e89 out.png         # a picture of it
./bench click 2e7e7e89 "button.go"    # click, type, submit — through the page's own events
./bench probe                         # the window's state: open panels, a modal, every window
./bench close all
```

Bench tabs are never selected for you, never enter the session or the history, and go when the script says so. It is how this browser is tested while somebody is using it.

An agent can drive an isolated copy of Search through `./bench-mcp`, an MCP server over the same socket. Run `./build.sh` from the repository root first, then register the server with your client:

```sh
claude mcp add search-bench -- "$PWD/bench-mcp"
codex mcp add search-bench -- "$PWD/bench-mcp"
agy mcp add --type stdio search-bench "$PWD/bench-mcp"
```

Each session starts this checkout's `build/Search.app` hidden, in a test world of its own, and wipes that world when it closes; the browser you use is never in reach. Its tools read a page as roles and names, or as an outline of its sections to open one at a time, click with real mouse events, type and check what the field holds, and wait on a condition, and a handle that has gone stale or a button that is covered is an error, never a guess. `python3 Tests/bench_mcp.py` checks it end to end.

To let an agent use the Search you have open instead, turn on Settings › About › Developer › Let coding agents use Search, and give it `./search-mcp`: `claude mcp add search -- "$PWD/search-mcp"`. Search asks you in the window each time one connects, shows a pill with Stop while it is there, and keeps it to tabs of its own; the rules are in `Sources/Search/AgentControl.swift`, and `python3 Tests/agent_control.py` checks them in a hidden probe.

`python3 Tests/split_view.py`, after `./build.sh`, checks Split View through the app's own model in a hidden test run with its own settings and files, all removed afterwards. It never makes or shows a window; what can only be seen (dragging onto a page's edge, the divider under the pointer, the motion) is checked by hand on a release candidate.

### Contributing

Issues and pull requests are genuinely welcome — see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for how this is reviewed and what tends to get merged. The short version: small changes, no new dependencies, nothing that phones home. Found a security problem? Please report it privately, as [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) says.

### License

MIT — see [LICENSE](LICENSE). Do what you want with the code. "Search" and the app icon are Office Commun's; please rename a fork before distributing it under another name.

repositories.name: OpenSpec
repositories.description: Spec-driven development (SDD) for AI coding assistants.
repositories.readme:
The most loved spec framework. [![Stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/Fission-AI/OpenSpec?style=flat-square&label=Stars)](https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/stargazers) [![Downloads](https://img.shields.io/npm/dm/@fission-ai/openspec?style=flat-square&label=Downloads/mo)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@fission-ai/openspec) [![Contributors](https://img.shields.io/github/contributors/Fission-AI/OpenSpec?style=flat-square&label=Contributors)](https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/graphs/contributors)

Our philosophy: ```text → fluid not rigid → iterative not waterfall → easy not complex → built for brownfield not just greenfield → scalable from personal projects to enterprises ```

Follow @0xTab on X for updates · Join the OpenSpec Discord for help and questions.

## See it in action ```text You: /openspec-explore AI: What would you like to explore? You: I want dark mode but I'm not sure how to do it cleanly. AI: Let me look at your styling setup... Cleanest path here: CSS variables + a small theme context, with system-preference detection. No new dependencies. Scope it? You: Yes, let's do it. You: /openspec-propose add-dark-mode AI: Created openspec/changes/add-dark-mode/ ✓ proposal.md — why we're doing this, what's changing ✓ specs/ — requirements and scenarios ✓ design.md — technical approach ✓ tasks.md — implementation checklist Ready for implementation! You: /openspec-apply-change AI: Implementing tasks... ✓ 1.1 Add theme context provider ✓ 1.2 Create toggle component ✓ 2.1 Add CSS variables ✓ 2.2 Wire up localStorage All tasks complete! You: /openspec-archive-change AI: Archived to openspec/changes/archive/2025-01-23-add-dark-mode/ Specs updated. Ready for the next feature. ```
What do the specs actually look like? Plain Markdown — requirements with concrete scenarios, no special syntax to learn. Here's what goes in the `specs/` folder created above: ```markdown ## ADDED Requirements ### Requirement: Theme selection The app SHALL let users switch between light and dark themes, defaulting to the system preference. #### Scenario: User toggles dark mode - **WHEN** the user clicks the theme toggle - **THEN** the app switches to dark mode and persists the choice ``` Your AI writes these; you review the plan before any code is written. OpenSpec is built with OpenSpec — browse this repo's live [specs](openspec/specs) and in-flight [changes](openspec/changes) for real examples at scale.
OpenSpec Dashboard

## Why teams adopt OpenSpec Solo, OpenSpec keeps you and your AI honest on a single repo. On a team, the hard part moves: a feature spans the API server, the web app, and a shared library; requirements are owned by one team and consumed by others; planning starts before any code exists. **[Stores](https://openspec.dev/docs/stores)** are the answer — planning in a repo of its own. The same `openspec/` shape you already know (specs and changes), shared by `git push` like anything else. One source of truth your whole team and every coding agent can read, across every repo. - **Cross-repo features** — one change, one plan, even when the code lands in three repos. - **Shared requirements** — a platform team owns the specs; product teams reference them read-only, right where their coding agent can read them. No drifting wiki. - **Plan before code** — capture the plan in the store now; the code repos catch up later. > Stores are in **beta**. Start with the [Stores guide](https://openspec.dev/docs/stores). ## Quick Start Install OpenSpec. On macOS or Linux, in your terminal: ```bash curl -fsSL https://openspec.dev/cli/install.sh | sh ``` On Windows, in PowerShell: ```powershell irm https://openspec.dev/cli/install.ps1 | iex ``` Prefer a package manager? `npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest` (needs Node.js 22.20.0 or higher) or the official [Homebrew formula](https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/openspec), `brew install openspec`. Then navigate to your project directory and initialize: ```bash cd your-project openspec init ``` > **Want your AI to do it?** Paste the [setup prompt](https://openspec.dev/docs/installation#install-with-your-ai-assistant) into your coding assistant — it installs the CLI, runs `openspec init`, and verifies the result. Now talk to your AI: - **Not sure what to build yet?** Start with `/openspec-explore`, a no-stakes thinking partner that reads your code, weighs options, and shapes a plan before any code gets written. ([Quickstart](https://openspec.dev/docs/quickstart)) - **Already know what you want?** Go straight to `/openspec-propose `. Both are in the default profile. If you want the expanded workflow (`openspec-new-change`, `openspec-continue-change`, `openspec-ff-change`, `openspec-verify-change`, `openspec-bulk-archive-change`, `openspec-onboard`), select it with `openspec config profile` and apply with `openspec update`. These are skills. Most tools invoke them as `/openspec-propose` and Codex as `$openspec-propose`, or you can ask for the work in plain words. `openspec init` prints the right form for the tools you picked — see [Supported Tools](https://openspec.dev/docs/supported-tools). Coming from 1.x and its `/opsx:*` commands? See [Upgrade to 2.0](https://openspec.dev/docs/upgrade-to-2). > [!NOTE] > Not sure if your tool is supported? [View the full list](https://openspec.dev/docs/supported-tools) – we support 30+ tools and growing. > > Also works with npm, Homebrew, pnpm, yarn, bun, and Nix. [See installation options](https://openspec.dev/docs/installation). ## Docs Full documentation lives at **[openspec.dev/docs](https://openspec.dev/docs)**. → **[Quickstart](https://openspec.dev/docs/quickstart)**: your first change, start to finish
→ **[Set up your project](https://openspec.dev/docs/setup)**: what `openspec init` installs
→ **[CLI](https://openspec.dev/docs/cli)**: terminal reference
→ **[Supported Tools](https://openspec.dev/docs/supported-tools)**: tool integrations & install paths
→ **[Customize](https://openspec.dev/docs/customize)**: profiles, project config, and schemas
→ **[Stores](https://openspec.dev/docs/stores)**: plan in a separate repo, shared across your team (beta)
→ **[Community Showcase](docs/community.md)**: projects and resources built with and for OpenSpec ## Community schemas Third-party schema bundles distributed via standalone repositories — these provide opinionated workflows that integrate OpenSpec with other tools, similar to how [github/spec-kit's community extension catalog](https://github.com/github/spec-kit/tree/main/extensions) handles tool integrations. → **[Browse the catalog](docs/customization.md#community-schemas)** in the customization docs. ## Why OpenSpec? AI coding assistants are powerful but unpredictable when requirements live only in chat history. OpenSpec adds a lightweight spec layer so you agree on what to build before any code is written. - **Agree before you build** — human and AI align on specs before code gets written - **Stay organized** — each change gets its own folder with proposal, specs, design, and tasks - **Work fluidly** — update any artifact anytime, no rigid phase gates - **Use your tools** — works with 30+ AI assistants via skills ### How we compare **vs. [Spec Kit](https://github.com/github/spec-kit)** (GitHub) — Thorough but heavyweight. Rigid phase gates, lots of Markdown, Python setup. OpenSpec is lighter and lets you iterate freely. **vs. [Kiro](https://kiro.dev)** (AWS) — Powerful but you're locked into their IDE and limited to Claude models. OpenSpec works with the tools you already use. **vs. nothing** — AI coding without specs means vague prompts and unpredictable results. OpenSpec brings predictability without the ceremony. ## Updating OpenSpec **Upgrade the CLI** With the standalone install, run `openspec install`. If you installed with npm: ```bash npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest ``` If you installed OpenSpec with Homebrew: ```bash brew upgrade openspec ``` **Refresh agent instructions** Run this once to refresh the skills installed on your machine. If your team keeps skills in Git, run it in each project that commits them. ```bash openspec update ``` ## Usage Notes **Model selection**: OpenSpec works best with high-reasoning models. We recommend Codex 5.5 and Opus 4.7 for both planning and implementation. **Context hygiene**: OpenSpec benefits from a clean context window. Clear your context before starting implementation and maintain good context hygiene throughout your session. ## Contributing Every change starts as an issue. We discuss it there, and if we agree to pursue it, a maintainer implements the change or invites you to build it with us. → **[CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md)**: the full process, from first issue to merged PR ## Other
Telemetry OpenSpec collects anonymous usage stats. We collect only command names and version to understand usage patterns. No arguments, paths, content, or PII. Automatically disabled in CI. **Opt-out (any one is enough):** - `openspec config set telemetry.enabled false` (global config; unset means on) - `export OPENSPEC_TELEMETRY=0` or `export DO_NOT_TRACK=1` (env overrides config)
Maintainers & Advisors See [MAINTAINERS.md](MAINTAINERS.md) for the list of core maintainers and advisors who help guide the project.

# Mailflare A self-hosted alternative to Google Workspace. Setup **custom domain Emails**, **Calendar, Drive, Booking** and **built-in AI agents**. Self-host it on Cloudflare or Docker. **Or try [Mailflare Cloud](https://cloud.mailflare.co?ref=github) with high-deliverable emails** from $4​ [![Deploy to Cloudflare](https://deploy.workers.cloudflare.com/button)](https://deploy.workers.cloudflare.com/?url=https://github.com/hieunc229/mailflare) ## Screenshots

Inbox
Domains
Mailboxes

Calendar
Booking
Drive
## Features ### Apps - **Email**: Custom domain mailboxes, personal or shared, with access you control. Send and receive with Cloudflare Email, Resend or Amazon SES. - **Routing rules**: Store, forward, reject or sort incoming mail, including a one-rule filter for newsletters and promotions. - **Calendar**: Repeating events with time zones. Attendees get email invitations. - **Booking**: Share a public link so anyone can book a free time on your calendar. - **Drive**: Store and share files. - **AI agents**: Search mail, draft replies and manage events. Connect other AI tools over MCP. ### Technical - **Databases**: Cloudflare D1 (default), PostgreSQL, MySQL, Turso / libSQL, or a local SQLite file. Set `DATABASE_URL` to switch. Works with Supabase, Neon, PlanetScale, TiDB and more. See [Databases](docs/databases.md). - **File storage**: Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2 or AWS S3. - **Hosting**: Cloudflare Workers or a single Docker container. - **Admin**: Users, API keys, webhooks, audit logs and backups. - **Import**: Bring in mail from IMAP, Gmail Takeout, `.eml` and `.mbox` files, and Google Calendar events, Google Contacts and Google Drive files from Takeout. See [Importing from Google Takeout](docs/import.md). Mailflare currently supports 34 languages, including English, Português (Brasil), Português (Portugal), Español, Français, Deutsch, Italiano, Nederlands, Polski, Українська, Русский, Türkçe, 中文（简体）, 日本語, 한국어, Bahasa Indonesia, Bahasa Melayu, Tiếng Việt, ไทย, हिन्दी, বাংলা, मराठी, తెలుగు, தமிழ், ગુજરાતી, ಕನ್ನಡ, മലയാളം, ਪੰਜਾਬੀ, සිංහල, Kiswahili, Hausa, plus العربية, اردو and فارسی (right-to-left). ## Cost You can receive and send mail for free. - **Receiving**: Cloudflare Email Routing is free. - **Sending**: Use the free tier of Resend (3,000 emails a month) or Amazon SES. Cloudflare's own sending needs the $5/month Paid Worker plan. New Amazon SES accounts start in a sandbox. Ask AWS for production access to lift it. Prices change, so check [Resend](https://resend.com/pricing), [Amazon SES](https://aws.amazon.com/ses/pricing/) and [Cloudflare](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/). ## Deploy 1. **Deploy the app.** Click **Deploy to Cloudflare**. Keep the app name `mailflare`, or it will break. 2. **Finish setup.** Open the app at `/setup` and create your admin account. 3. **Connect a domain.** Add a domain from the same Cloudflare account, then create your first mailbox. > **`CF_TOKEN` is required.** Create a scoped [Cloudflare API token](https://github.com/hieunc229/mailflare/issues/24#issuecomment-5523686105) with these permissions: > > - All accounts: Email Sending:Edit, DNS Settings:Edit, Email Routing Addresses:Edit > - All zones: DNS Settings:Edit, Email Routing Rules:Edit, Zone Settings:Edit, DNS:Edit More options: [deployment guide](docs/deployment.md). ### Deploy with an AI agent Paste this into an AI agent that has terminal access (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and similar): ```text Install Mailflare for me from https://github.com/hieunc229/mailflare on my Cloudflare account. 1. Read README.md, docs/deployment.md and wrangler.jsonc first. 2. Ask me for my Cloudflare account ID and two API tokens, using a secret input: a deploy token (for Wrangler) and a runtime token (the Worker secret CF_TOKEN). Never print them, commit them, or pass them as command arguments. 3. Keep the Worker name exactly "mailflare". Create or reuse the D1 database "mailflare", the R2 bucket "mailflare-raw", and the queues "mailflare-inbound", "mailflare-outbound" and "mailflare-agent". 4. Install dependencies, run `npm run deploy`, and set CF_TOKEN as a Worker secret. Do not run remote database migrations yourself. The /setup page does that. 5. Give me the app URL and anything I still need to do. I will open /setup, create the admin account and connect my domain. ``` Token permissions and more options: [deployment guide](docs/deployment.md#deploy-with-an-ai-coding-agent). ### Self-host with Docker Runs as one container on any server, with SQLite and local files. ```bash cp .env.docker.example .env.docker docker compose up -d --build ``` Or skip the build and run the prebuilt image: `docker compose -f docker-compose.image.yml up -d`. See [self-hosting](docs/self-hosting.md). ## Local development ```bash cp .dev.vars.example .dev.vars npm install npm run db:migrate:local npm run dev ``` Add your Cloudflare credentials to `.dev.vars`, then open [localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000). Run `npm run db:seed` to load sample data. - `npm run build`: build the Worker - `npm run deploy`: build and deploy - `npm run lint`: lint and type check A schema change needs a migration for each database type. See [Databases](docs/databases.md#migrations). ## Documentation - [Deployment and configuration](docs/deployment.md) - [Databases](docs/databases.md) - [Sending and receiving providers](docs/providers.md) - [API and integrations](docs/api.md) - [Email assistant and MCP](docs/email-assistant-and-mcp.md) - [Importing from Google Takeout](docs/import.md) - [Adding a language](docs/localization.md) - [Troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md) ## License See [LICENSE](LICENSE).
